title: Found While Looking For Something Else
logline: A small cave shrine in which every remarkable thing arrived by accident, and the most remarkable of them is a low altar at the foot of a nine-metre reclining figure, faced with about two hundred blue-and-white tiles made on the other side of the world, each one carrying a scene from somebody else's scripture, and a good many of them laid sideways.
human_question: If nothing here was found by anybody who was looking for it, and nothing on this surface tells me which way up it was meant to be, how much of what I am certain I am seeing did I bring in with me?

place.what_kind_of_place: A working temple built into a natural rock cave on a low grey hill, reached on foot up a short flight of steps from a courtyard, in dry-zone hill country of no great height and no great view. It is small. The whole complex is a stone image house of eight carved pillars, an entrance hall with an enormous old alms bowl in it, the cave shrine itself with a reclining figure about nine metres long and a gilded seated figure kept under glass, an upper shrine of three chambers added in the eighteenth century, an ivory-framed doorway, a semicircular moonstone, and two small stupas, one of them on a separate rock reached by its own granite steps. The cave's roof is plastered and painted, and the plaster is fragile: a large section of it came down in one pilgrimage season within living memory. And at the foot of the reclining figure, on the low altar where flowers are set, there are the tiles: hand-width, blue on white, glazed, chipped at the corners, about two hundred of them, each one a picture of an episode from the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, laid in an order that follows nothing in the pictures.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: One subject, and it is a hand's width across. A raking morning light coming in low through the shrine opening crosses a tiled surface at almost no angle at all, which is exactly the light that makes a glaze legible: the crazing, the pooled blue at the edge of a brushstroke, the bevel where two tiles meet, the chip taken off a corner two centuries ago. Move along that surface slowly and the film is a reading: a garden, a flood, a bird with a branch, a bush on fire, a last meal, a figure lying on its side because the tile was set on its side, a scene upside down. Then lift the camera off it by a metre and every one of those stories vanishes into a field of blue and white, which is the only thing the surface was ever asked to be. The rest of the film is dim, small and close by design — a nine-metre figure held in one static frame from floor level, an ivory door frame, a carved moonstone — and none of it needs a vista, a drone or a change of weather.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Very little, and what does move is light and flowers, neither of which the crew touches. The low sun through the opening reaches along the altar in one short window and then leaves it; for most of the day the tiles are simply dark blue and unreadable, which is a fact worth filming. Flowers left on the altar go over in a day, so the surface under them is never the same twice, and nobody is filmed putting them there. Otherwise the change in this film is the camera's own movement along a surface, one lateral pass, slow enough to read: the only sustained move in the whole thing. There is no reveal, no climb and no payoff shot. The payoff is the move off the surface, when the pictures stop being pictures.
place.when_it_looks_best: First light on an ordinary weekday, out of the pilgrimage season and never on a full-moon observance day. The whole film depends on low sun raking along the tiles through the shrine's opening, so the window is short, it is at one end of the day, and it needs a clear morning; the raking pass has no substitute in flat light. Nothing else here depends on the season, the weather or the month, and the interiors have to be exposed on available light, which means the dim stretches are shot at whatever they actually are.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: The smallest film on the slate and the only one whose whole subject is a single made object. It opens outside on a low grey hill in flat light, goes in through a stone porch and an entrance hall, finds a room with a very long figure lying down in it, and then goes to the floor and stays there: one slow pass along a low tiled altar, close enough to read every picture on it, followed by macro on single tiles — glaze, crazing, a chipped corner, the blue. It ends by lifting a metre off the surface, at which point the two hundred stories collapse into a pattern. It resolves on its own terms, from a hill to a hand's width and back out again, and works with no narration at all as a piece about one object nobody expected to find in this room.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' account of how a mind gets hold of anything. The books give six factors that come and go: aiming at an object, going over it, settling on it, pushing on, the lift, and the wish to take it up. The film uses three. The chronicle's own chapter about this place is a chapter of seven accidents in which nobody found what he set out for — which is the first factor, the one the books picture as another man lifting onto your shoulder a load you could not lift alone. The tiles are the third factor: a surface on which two hundred settled meanings were taken up for a different one and laid down in whatever orientation a hand happened to hold them, over which the books say something a camera confirms at once — the settling factor grips firmly without sorting true from false, and is very often wrong while being perfectly firm, and is hard to notice at all. And the voice never says that anybody here was wrong, because the books put that clause on the factor and not on a person. Then the feeling books take the last step: the pain anybody can see, they say, can be known without asking, and the other kind is called concealed for the reason that it has to be asked for. Two hundred pictures of other people's worst and best days are lying flat in this room, and the film's instrument has never asked anybody anything.

sequence.on_screen: Flat early light outside. A low grey rock hill, held in one static ground-level frame, with nothing monumental in it. Then a stone image house of eight carved pillars, and a dark doorway.
sequence.voice: The chronicle that carries this story tells it as a chapter of finds, and not one of the finders was looking for what he found. A huntsman went into the forest with his dogs, chased an iguana, and came on a stack of bricks. Fishermen found pearls lying on dry ground. And a merchant loaded his wagons and set out for ginger.

sequence.on_screen: Inside the stone porch: the eight pillars in raking light, carved figures at eye level, the ceiling low. A slow pan across them, then a held frame on the empty hall and a very large old alms bowl standing in it.
sequence.voice: He stopped short of a hill because he needed wood to cut whip handles. Up there he found a branch of a fruit tree bearing one fruit the size of a water pitcher, and he cut it down. Then he did something the chronicle records almost in passing: with faith, he announced the meal time. Eight monks came, in two groups of four. He gave the juice to four of them and the seeds to four more, and seven of them walked away.

sequence.on_screen: The cave shrine's mouth, and the fall-off of light behind it. Then inside: the whole length of the reclining figure in one static frame from floor level, exposed on what comes through the opening, the far end of it almost gone.
sequence.voice: The eighth one did not. He walked further down the hill, sat near the mouth of a cave, ate his seeds, and waited to be followed. Then he opened a path and said: go this way now. The merchant struck the rock with his axe, found silver in it, left his wagons where they stood and carried one lump of it to the king. The books this series reads have a name for the first of the six things that come and go in a working mind: the one that gets hold of a thing at all. Their picture for it is a second man helping you lift onto your shoulder a load you could not have lifted alone.

sequence.on_screen: Down to the floor. The low altar at the foot of the reclining figure, in the first raking light: one slow lateral pass along the tiled face, close enough to read each tile, nothing touched or cleaned.
sequence.voice: Then, at some point in the eighteenth century, about two hundred tiles arrived in this room from the other side of the world. They are Dutch, they are eighteenth-century, and each one carries an episode from the Hebrew and Christian scriptures: a garden and an expulsion from it, a flood and a bird with a branch, a bush on fire, a last meal. How they got here is not written down in any record anybody has found. A king who was repairing this temple is said to have been given them. That is as far as the evidence goes, and the film goes no further than the evidence.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, available light, one tile at a time: glaze, crazing, the pooled blue at the end of a brushstroke, a corner chipped away. Then four in a row, and the orientation changing — a figure lying on its side, a scene inverted.
sequence.voice: The third of the six factors is the deciding one: the thing that settles on an object in one way instead of going two or three ways about it. The books are blunt about what it does. It takes hold firmly without sorting true from false or good from bad. It is very often wrong while being completely firm. And they add that it is one of the hard ones to notice happening. Two hundred pictures came here already decided, and were taken up for something else, and were set down whichever way a hand was holding them. Nothing on this surface tells you which way up anything was meant.

sequence.on_screen: The long flat middle. The altar in full, with flowers already on it, and the light leaving it minute by minute until the blue goes dark and the pictures are no longer legible. No one in frame.
sequence.voice: Something has to be said about this part, because it looks like nothing is happening. The books teach that every mind is tasting whatever it has taken hold of, and that the taste comes three ways with no fourth: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither one. Of all the kinds of moment they count, fifty-five carry the neither. That is not an empty count and it is not numbness — the same neither runs through the most refined states in their whole scheme. An hour in front of a surface going dark has a feeling in it.

sequence.on_screen: The closest frames in the film: a single tile filling the frame, a figure in it a thumbnail across. Then the camera lifts a metre off the surface and every picture disappears into a field of blue and white.
sequence.voice: The same books split pain in two, and the split is not where a film usually puts it. One kind, they say, anybody can see, because the means of it is out in the open — their examples are beatings and being shut up. The other kind is a head, a tooth, a mind burning; and the reason they call that kind concealed is given in their own sentence. It has to be asked for. There are two hundred pictures of other people's worst days and best days lying flat in this room, and the thing looking at them has never asked anybody anything.

sequence.on_screen: Out through the porch. The stupa on its separate rock, from below, in flat light, one static frame. Then the low grey hill again, and the shrine's dark opening in it.
sequence.voice: The books draw one more line and it is the one this group exists for. The wish to take a thing up is one item. The grip that will not let go is a different item, and they give it its own names. Trained, they say, the wish to take a thing up is what carries a person as far as they are capable of going. A man wanted ginger. He gave away a fruit. What the chronicle sets down after that is a list of what turned up, and what any of it came to mean to anybody is the one thing neither the chronicle nor this altar can hand over.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C021 is a description of how a mind takes hold of an object and C032 is a description of what that costs the person holding it, and this site stages the first as documented history and the second as a limit on the camera. C021 names six factors that come and go — initial application, sustained application, decision, effort, rapture and desire-to-act — and insists first of all that not one of them is good or bad in itself, since each takes the moral colour of whatever mind it joins [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L29]. The film uses three of the six and leaves three alone. It uses initial application, whose defining work is to raise the mind onto an object, and whose coarse simile is another man helping you lift onto your shoulder a burden you could not have lifted by yourself [C021-P:L33]; the Margaya glosses the same factor as the effort that reaches places the mind has not reached and knows what was not known [C021-M:L7]. It uses decision, which settles on an object without sorting true from false or good from bad, holds it firmly, and 'very often believes wrongly, taking the untrue as true' [C021-P:L45], and which the Margaya calls hard to discern and says lets the mind take the object in some one way, rightly or wrongly, rather than going two or three ways about it [C021-M:L15]. And it ends on desire-to-act, which the Pradeepika defines as the wish to take the object up and not the power that makes one cling to it, the clinging being given its own names [C021-P:L69], which the Margaya puts as a wanting with none of greed's adhesion in it [C021-M:L27], and which developed is said to help subdue craving and to carry a person to the highest good [C021-P:L75]. C032 then supplies two things the footage cannot. First a floor under the film's long unlit stretch: feeling is present in every mind because every mind arises taking an object [C032-P:L43], it is threefold by the way the object's flavour is experienced and there is no fourth way [C032-M:L5] [C032-P:L52], and fifty-five of the minds counted carry the neutral one [C032-M:L13], which is not numbness. Second, and this is why the pairing is not decorative, the source's own reason that one kind of suffering is called concealed: pains of the head, the teeth, the limbs, and a mind burning with desire or hatred, must be known by asking, and their cause is not manifest [C032-P:L119], where the afflictions that come from outside — violence, confinement — are knowable without asking because the means is plain [C032-P:L121]. A room whose remarkable object is two hundred pictures of other people's extremity, laid flat where flowers are put, is the place to say that out loud, and to say it about the instrument rather than about anybody in the room.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the chronicle's story and the tiles are the same story told twice, and that neither of them is about wanting the wrong thing. C021 alone would make this a film about craft or attention. C032 alone would be a classification with nowhere to stand. Together they produce the one argument this place can make and no other site on the slate can: an object arrives already decided, and what it turns out to be is settled by something other than the object. The chronicle records seven finds and not one finder who was looking for what he found — the raising of the mind onto its object done entirely from outside, which is the source's own simile for that factor and not an analogy anybody had to build. The tiles are the same thing a second time and closer to hand: pictures made to mean one thing, taken up to be a surface, and set down in whatever orientation a hand was holding them. The pairing also closes the two exits this film would otherwise take. It cannot be a film about a mistake, because the source puts the wrongness on the factor and not on a person — the decision factor is 'often wrong while being firm' as a general fact about minds, and the digest's own refusal of 'trust your gut, if you're sure it's right' is the line being illustrated, not a verdict on whoever laid this surface. And it cannot be a film about what any of this meant to anyone, because C032 states the reason: the kind of experience that would answer that question is the kind that has to be asked for, and a camera does not ask. So the film's last move is off the surface rather than into it.

concept_links.why: Three of the six factors are documented history at this site rather than illustrated by it, and the digest's own limits decide which three. Initial application is defined as the nature that brings the mind and its co-arisen factors to the object and raises them onto it, and the Pradeepika's simile for it is another person helping you lift onto your shoulder a load you could not lift alone, with the hawk beating its wings to climb standing beside it [C021-P:L33]; the Margaya's gloss is the effort to reach where the mind has not reached and to know what was not known [C021-M:L7]. The chronicle's chapter on this place is that factor as a list of events: a huntsman after an iguana finding bricks, fishermen finding pearls on dry land, a merchant on his way to buy ginger being led to silver by somebody else. Nobody in it lifted his own object onto his own mind, which is the simile's whole content. Decision is the second use and it is what the tiles are for. The Pradeepika says it settles the object, helps the mind stand firm on it without doubt, and — without distinguishing true, false, good or bad — takes hold of whatever the object may be and establishes it, and that it very often does this wrongly, holding the untrue as true, which is what is meant by mithyadhimokkha [C021-P:L45]; the Margaya adds that because of this factor the mind does not go two or three ways but takes the object in some one way, rightly or wrongly, and that it is a hard-to-discern, unobvious factor [C021-M:L15]. Both clauses are about the factor. The digest's does_not_transfer line 'trust your gut, if you're sure it's right' is exactly this, and it is the reason the film can put a surface of misoriented pictures on screen without accusing the person who laid them: the wrongness the source names is structural, not somebody's failing, and no beat says anyone here was ignorant, mistaken or careless. Desire-to-act is the third and it carries the ending. The Pradeepika is explicit that it is the wish to take the object and not the power that makes one cling there, that power having its own names, and that by this factor only the taking of the object happens, without regard to good or bad [C021-P:L69]; the Margaya says it looks a little like greed but has none of greed's adhesion, and that in greed-accompanied minds it accords with greed while in minds opposed to greed it opposes it [C021-M:L27]; developed into a predominant factor and a base of success it is said to subdue craving and lead to the highest good [C021-P:L75]. In a group about the greed-rooted minds that distinction is the whole permission for a film about a man who wanted ginger. Three further limits are honoured by omission. Effort is not used as a theme at all, because the digest refuses 'hard work is always virtuous' and the Pradeepika's own image has effort running downhill as easily as up, like a boat on a current in a mind already leaning towards harm [C021-P:L53]; there is no patient-craft register anywhere in this film. Rapture is not used, since the digest records its bodily and air-element account as traditional physiology [C021-P:L61], and no beat reads a state off anybody. And the overriding clause is stated in the first line of the concept: these factors take the colour of the mind they join and are not virtues [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L29], so nothing here is offered as an example of a good mind. One uncertainty is recorded rather than leaned on: the digest notes that C021-M:L7 carries an unmatched closing quotation mark so the extent of that quotation is unclear, and the film uses the sentence's plain sense and does not quote it.

It does two jobs and is kept off a third. First it puts a floor under the film's long unlit stretch, which is otherwise the weakest thing in the record. Feeling is the experiencing of the object's flavour and the name for dividing mind and mental factors by it [C032-P:L41]; because every mind arises taking an object, the power of experiencing that object's flavour arises in every mind, and differs with the object's own nature [C032-P:L43]; by the way the flavour is experienced it is threefold, sweet, unsweet and middling, and the Margaya says outright that there is no other way besides these three [C032-M:L5] [C032-P:L52]; and fifty-five of the minds counted carry the neutral one [C032-M:L13] against sixty-two carrying gladness [C032-M:L9]. Beat 6 is that count spoken over an altar going dark, and the digest's 'neutral means numb' warning is the reason the beat exists at all, since the same neutral feeling appears in greed-rooted minds and in the most refined meditative ones. Second, and this is the concept's real contribution, it supplies the film's limit on itself. The Pradeepika divides suffering into the concealed and the open: pains of the hand, foot, head, teeth and ears and the burnings of the mind that come of desire and hatred are called concealed because these bodily and mental afflictions have to be known by asking and their cause is not manifest [C032-P:L119], while the various afflictions that arrive from outside — torment, violence, confinement — are called open because they can be known without asking, the means being plain [C032-P:L121]. Beat 7 says that over two hundred pictures of scriptural extremity and turns it onto the camera, which only ever gets the second kind. That is the one charge in this digest that lands on looking rather than on anybody in frame, and it is used exactly once. Three things are refused. The Pradeepika's own wording for the neutral object [C032-P:L75] is flagged in the digest as reading like a moderately pleasing object and as possibly garbled and needing an expert check, so the film uses the counts and the threefold scheme and never that definition. The group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins is recorded in the digest as editorial compression rather than a sentence in these extracts, and it is never spoken. And the teaching that all conditioned feeling counts as suffering in three senses [C032-P:L111], including the suffering of change by which pleasant feelings become causes of pain when they turn [C032-P:L117] and the suffering of conditioned rise and fall [C032-P:L115], is not carried into the narration at all: the digest notes it rests on the Pradeepika alone and warns against 'life is suffering' as pessimism and against 'chase good vibes' as its inverse, and a film about a room where flowers are laid has no business making either point. The digest's separation of bodily pain, whose single seat is touch [C032-P:L103] [C032-P:L95-L97], from mental displeasure is noted and not used, because nobody's body is in this film.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the thing a mind ends up holding is very often not the thing it set out for, and that this is ordinary rather than a failure — the books' own picture for the factor that gets hold of an object is somebody else lifting the load onto your shoulder. That wanting to take a thing up and being unable to let it go are two separate items with separate names, which is the distinction this whole group is built on. That an hour in which nothing appears to be happening still has a feeling in it, and that the feeling being neither pleasant nor unpleasant does not make it an absence. And, from the last two minutes, that what a surface meant to anyone who ever knelt at it is not recoverable by looking at the surface, because the sources say in as many words that the hidden kind of experience has to be asked for.
what_must_be_real: The tiles as they lie. Nothing is cleaned, wetted, chalked, oiled, rubbed, re-laid, re-lit or touched in any way: they are a two-hundred-year-old glazed surface on a working altar and the camera does not make contact with them. No frame in this film is lit. The raking pass is made on whatever low sun actually comes through the opening on the morning it is filmed, and a frame that cannot be exposed on available light is lost rather than lit; the plastered and painted cave roof and the glazed tiles both rule out flash and every substitute for it. No act of worship is filmed, interrupted, restarted, arranged, waited out in frame or lit, and no offering is made, moved or set for the camera; the flowers on the altar are whatever flowers are on it. Nobody in this building is a subject or an example. No face is held, nobody is followed, nobody is asked to explain, react or say why they came, and nobody appears who could not step away from a camera if they wanted to — which in a small shrine means the room is filmed when it is empty and the film is abandoned for the day rather than filmed around people. The resident community's permission is the condition of the whole thing and is asked for in their own terms, with what the film is and where it will be seen stated plainly and more than once. The scriptural scenes on the tiles are filmed as what they are and never as a curiosity, a joke or an exotic detail. The film states once, factually, that the tiles are Dutch, eighteenth-century, and that no record of how they arrived has been found, and it does not narrate their presence as tolerance, as irony, as a lesson about empires or as anything's comeuppance. No king's merit is narrated. What the chronicle records is what was found and by whom; what it was worth to anybody, in this life or another, is outside the film.
position_hint: Early-middle in the group: the smallest-scale film on the slate and the only one whose whole subject is one imported object a hand's width across. It works best after a film that has shown wanting at the scale of a town or a saturated room, so that a single tile reads as a reduction rather than as a detail, and before the group's long cold and empty films, which need the audience's patience rather than supplying it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Making the tiler wrong. The source's clause is about the factor, not a person: the deciding factor takes hold without sorting true from false and very often holds the untrue as true [C021-P:L45], and the Margaya says it settles the object in some one way, rightly or wrongly, and is hard to discern [C021-M:L15]. The digest's own refusal of 'trust your gut, if you're sure it's right' is that sentence. The widely repeated inference that whoever laid these tiles did not know what the pictures were is an inference in the travel and heritage literature, not a record, and no beat states or implies it.

Narrating the Dutch tiles as tolerance, as coexistence, as irony or as an empire's pictures put in their place. The row forbids it and the record cannot support any of it: no document for the gift has been found, the period includes open war between this kingdom and the Dutch Company and a treaty ceding the coast to it, and adjudicating any of that would breach the standing rule that colonial and contested history is recorded as layers and never adjudicated. The film states the object and the gap in the record, once, flat.

Narrating a king's merit. The chronicle's own chapter on the seven finds closes on a verse about merit heaped up with a believing heart, and the temple's foundation story is a merit story from end to end. The film uses the chapter for what was found and by whom and goes nowhere near what it was worth to anyone, which the row requires and which kamma-is-not-fate requires anyway.

Offering the six factors as virtues. The Pradeepika's first sentence on them is that they take the moral colour of the mind they join [C021-P:L25], and the Margaya says the same [C021-M:L29]. Nothing in this film reads a good mind off anybody, alive or dead.

Drifting into effort as a theme. The digest refuses 'hard work is always virtuous' and the Pradeepika's image has effort running downhill as easily as up, like a boat on a downstream current in a mind already inclined to harm [C021-P:L53]. There is no patient-craft register in this film and no admiration of anybody's labour.

'Follow your passion', which the digest names: desire-to-act inside a greed-rooted mind strengthens greed [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27], so nothing here presents a wish as self-justifying. Its mirror, 'desire is the enemy', is refused by the same lines and is the reason beat 8 exists.

Reading a state off a body. Rapture's bodily account [C021-P:L61] is recorded in the digest as traditional physiology, and no beat in this film puts a mental factor onto anybody's face, posture or gesture.

'Neutral means numb', which the digest rules out by name: the same neutral feeling runs through greed-rooted minds and through the most refined states in the scheme [C032-M:L13]. Beat 6 exists to refuse it and must not be allowed to become a beat about calm or equanimity.
Speaking the group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins. The digest is explicit that this is editorial compression and not a sentence in these extracts, and it is never spoken.
Using the Pradeepika's wording for the neutral object [C032-P:L75], which the digest flags as reading like a moderately pleasing object, as possibly garbled, and as needing an expert check.

Carrying the threefold suffering into the narration — the suffering of conditioned rise and fall [C032-P:L115] and the suffering of change by which a pleasure becomes a cause of pain when it turns [C032-P:L117]. The digest notes it rests on the Pradeepika alone and warns against both 'life is suffering' as pessimism and 'chase good vibes' as its inverse. A room where flowers are laid is the wrong place to make either point and the film makes neither.

Treating scriptural scenes as an exotic curio. Two hundred tiles of somebody's sacred narrative are on a working altar in somebody else's living shrine. They are filmed as objects on that altar, described accurately, and never played for surprise, comedy or contrast.

Physical damage. The plaster on this cave roof has already come down once in a crowded season, the tiles are chipped and crazed, and the ivory carving has been vandalised in the past. Nothing is touched, no tripod leg goes on the altar or its platform, and no light is put near a painted or glazed surface.

Consent in a small room. This is a shrine a few metres across with a single approach, so a person inside it cannot step out of frame. The film is therefore made in an empty room and abandons a session rather than filming around anybody.

Becoming a heritage documentary. The phases, the dynasties, the four inscription groups and the restoration history are the location's research, not the film's content. The voice carries one chronicle chapter and one object.

Smoothing the figures. The tile count, the placement of the tiles, the list of scenes, the temple's founder, the distance from the district town and even the published coordinates all differ between sources, and the differences are kept apart in the location's disputed block rather than averaged. No count is spoken except 'about two hundred', which is what the two most careful sources say and is stated as approximate.

Repeating the group's other cave shrine. That film is five shelters, saturation, scale, a ceiling and the one thing left unpainted, on three different concepts; this one is one small room, one imported object a hand's width across, a low surface at floor level rather than a ceiling, a lateral pass rather than a tilt, and the thing that is wrongly oriented rather than the thing left plain. They share no shot, no argument and no concept.
drop_if: The altar and its tiles cannot be filmed at all. The film's central shot has no substitute and there is no smaller version of this record that survives without it.
The tiles can only be read by adding light, or by cleaning, wetting or rubbing the glaze.
The raking morning light does not reach the altar face, or reaches it only on days when the shrine is full. This is checked on a pre-visit and the film is not attempted against it.
Filming cannot be done without people in a room they cannot step out of, or without a queue being held up past a shrine.
The resident community will not have a camera in the shrine, which is a real possibility and is not worked around.
Access is offered on condition that the tiles are presented as a curiosity, that the film supplies an account of how they arrived, or that it draws a moral about the two traditions.

connections.note: The group's two cave shrines, split on purpose and on different concepts. That one is saturation and scale — five shelters, a painted ceiling riding the rock's own shape, and the one surface nobody decorated. This one is small, has one made object in it, and looks down instead of up: a hand-width tile that arrived from the other side of the world already meaning something else. Each is the other's control, a room where everything was made beautiful against a room where the remarkable thing was brought in.

The group's two films on the same primary concept, using different factors out of the six and deliberately opposite cinema. That one is carved stone in flat high daylight, outdoors, on effort and a duration; this one is indoors, dim, at floor level, on the aiming and the deciding. Both refuse effort as a virtue, on the same digest line.

The group's other film carrying the feeling concept, and it carries the same load-bearing guard: the neutral feeling is not calm and not equanimity. That one holds it over two thousand metres of cloud and wet grass; this one holds it over a tiled surface going dark in a room a few metres across.

selection.reason: A destination whose documented history is a chapter of accidents, in which the chronicle's own account of how the material for a great stupa was found turns on the concept's own question — how a mind gets hold of an object it was not looking for. It is also the group's smallest film, its only one built on a single imported object, and its only one whose payoff is a move off a surface rather than a reveal of one.

review.note: Written fresh rather than patched, so the verdict is reset. The old film went for the exact reason the reassignment brief names: a street of hand gem-cutting benches is an honest working place that carried the concept only by analogy, because a bench happens to resemble the Pradeepika's simile of one hand gripping a vessel while the other rubs it over, and it had no chronicled, inscribed or disputed story in it at all. It also put a camera, in a group about the greed-rooted minds, on identifiable people working stones of real value for owners who are not themselves, at the point where the value is realised, which is the floor's problem and not a framing problem. The historical binding of the replacement is that the chronicle chapter about this place is not a story about silver, it is a list of seven accidents. Every material for the great stupa appears in one chapter and every finder was about other business: a huntsman went into the forest with dogs and chased an iguana and found bricks, fishermen found pearls on dry land, villagers found gold in the earth, and a merchant who had loaded wagons for ginger stopped short of a hill for whip-wood, cut down one fruit, gave it away to eight monks, was followed by the eighth, and was shown silver. That is C021's initial application as recorded history rather than as an image: the Pradeepika's simile for the factor that gets hold of an object is another man lifting onto your shoulder a load you could not lift alone, and nobody in that chapter lifted his own object. The site's other object does it again and nearer to hand. About two hundred eighteenth-century Dutch tiles, each carrying a scene from the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, face the low altar at the foot of a nine-metre reclining figure, and a good many of them are set sideways or inverted, so two hundred already-settled meanings were taken up for a different one and laid down in whatever orientation a hand held them. That is the decision factor, which the Pradeepika says grips firmly without sorting true from false and is very often wrong while being firm, and which the Margaya calls hard to discern. The research corrected the row's notes in several places and every correction is recorded in the location's disputed block. The chronicles do not say what they are cited for: Mahavamsa XXVIII records silver appearing in a named cave and contains no foundation of any temple there, while Mahavamsa XXXV records that it was Amandagamani Abhaya, in the first century AD, who built the monastery of the silver cave; the Dutugemunu-in-gratitude account, the three hundred stone craftsmen, the name Arahant Indragupta and the gilded image said to have been brought from overseas all come from later texts, chiefly a late Sinhala record of this temple's own founding and the Culavamsa as continued in the eighteenth century by a monk of this very temple. The gift of the tiles is unsourced in every account found — a Dutch governor, a Dutch envoy and a Dutch consul are all in circulation, none is named and no archive is cited, and one local magazine account says outright that the origin is undocumented. The tiles are on the flower altar and pedestal rather than being a floor as such, the count is given as about two hundred by two sources and as over a hundred by a third, the trade name usually attached to them is loose, since tiles of this kind were mostly made in other Dutch towns, and the published coordinates differ from the mapped ones by about 1.7 km. On the pattern the brief warned about, C032 turned out to hold the same kind of line the other writers found: its concealed suffering is concealed for the stated reason that it has to be asked for, which lands on looking rather than on anybody in frame, and beat 7 turns it onto the camera and uses it once. The guards: no artificial light anywhere, since the roof plaster and the glazed tiles both rule out flash and every substitute, so a frame that cannot be exposed on the low sun coming through the opening is lost; nothing on the altar touched, cleaned, wetted, chalked or re-laid, and no tripod on the platform; no worship filmed, interrupted, arranged or lit, and no offering set for the camera; nobody identifiable in frame at all, because a shrine a few metres across with one approach means a person inside it cannot refuse a camera, so the room is filmed empty and a session is abandoned rather than worked around; no king's merit narrated, and the chronicle's own closing merit verse left alone; the Dutch tiles never narrated as tolerance, irony or a lesson about empires, and the colonial layers recorded without being adjudicated; the scriptural scenes never played as a curiosity or a joke; nobody made wrong, because the source's wrongness clause is about the factor and not about whoever laid this surface; C032's neutral feeling never allowed to become calm or equanimity, and its threefold suffering left out of the narration altogether. Separation from the group's other cave shrine is total by construction: different concepts, one small room against five, a low altar face against a ceiling, a lateral pass against a tilt, one imported object against saturation, and a misoriented thing against an undecorated one. The record also notes that this location puts a sixth film in one district, which is a slate-level judgement for Chathura rather than something this rewrite can settle. Title, place, two_layers, an eight-beat sequence, concept_merge, both concept links, the risks, the drop conditions, the connections and the whole of suggested_location are new; the previous title is kept in aliases.

suggested_location.why_here: It hands this film both halves of the standard, and it does it at the only scale the concept can honestly be filmed at. The story is not a resemblance: the chronicle chapter that gives this place its name is a chapter of seven accidents in which nobody found what he set out for, and the concept's first factor is defined as the raising of the mind onto an object with the source's own simile being somebody else lifting the load for you. Then the site does it a second time in a single object. About two hundred eighteenth-century Dutch tiles, each carrying an episode from the Hebrew and Christian scriptures, face the low altar at the foot of a nine-metre reclining figure, a good many of them set sideways or upside down, and no record has been found of how they got here. That is the deciding factor made visible: two hundred settled meanings taken up for a different purpose and laid down in whatever orientation a hand was holding them, on a surface that will not tell you which way up anything was meant. Cinematically it is the slate's best small subject and the group's only film that looks down. A hand-width glazed tile in low raking light through a shrine opening gives crazing, pooled blue, a chipped corner and a figure lying on its side, all of it legible for one short window in the morning; and the single most beautiful movement the room produces — the lift off the surface, when two hundred stories dissolve into a field of blue and white — is also the clearest statement the concept can get, that what a thing turns out to be is settled by something other than the thing.

historical_thread.story:
The chronicle chapter that this temple's name comes from is chapter XXVIII of the Mahavamsa, and it is not really about silver. Dutthagamani Abhaya, having decided to build the Great Thupa at Anuradhapura, lay on his palace terrace worrying that he could not levy a tax on a people he had just fought a war over, and could not therefore have bricks made. What follows is a list of seven things that appeared, and in nearly every case they were found by somebody who was about other business or none. Bricks, prepared by Vissakamma at Sakka's order a yojana from the city, were found by a huntsman who had gone into the forest with his dogs and was chasing an iguana. Nuggets of gold, the largest a span and the smallest a finger's measure, appeared on a sixteen-karisa plain near Acaravitthigama and were noticed by the villagers. Copper appeared near Tambapittha, gems near the village of Sumanavapi, six waggonloads of pearls mingled with coral 'came forth to the dry land' at the landing-place Uruvela and were seen by fishermen, and four gems the size of a small mill-stone and the colour of flax-flowers formed in a cave above the sand at the Pelivapikagama tank, where a hunter with his dogs saw them. The king, in Geiger's translation, 'heard, on one and the same day, that the bricks and the other treasures had appeared'.

The silver is the fourth item on that list, and it is the only one the chapter tells as a story. 'In a southerly direction from the city, at a distance of eight yojanas, silver appeared in the Ambatthakola-cave.' A merchant from the city had taken many waggons and set out for Malaya in order to bring back ginger and so forth. Not far from the cave he halted the waggons, and 'since he had need of wood for whips he went up that mountain'. There he saw a branch of a bread-fruit tree bearing one single fruit as large as a waterpitcher and dragged down by its weight. He cut the fruit from the stalk with his knife, and 'thinking: I will give the first produce as alms, with faith he announced the meal time'. Four theras free from the asavas came; he seated them, cut away the rind, tore out the bottom of the fruit, poured the juice into their bowls and gave them the four bowls, and they accepted them and went their way. He announced the meal time again, and four other theras appeared; he filled their bowls with the kernels. Three of those went their way, and one did not. 'In order to show him the silver he went further down and seating himself near the cave he ate the kernels.' The merchant finished the kernels that were left, bundled up the rest, followed the thera's track, found him, and paid him the usual attentions. 'The thera opened a path for him to the mouth of the cavern: Go thou now also on this path, lay brother!' The merchant did reverence, went that way, saw the cave, struck the silver with his axe, knew it for silver, took a lump, went back to his freight-waggons, left them there and went in haste to the capital and showed the king. Not one word of that passage has the merchant looking for silver, and the chapter closes on a verse about merit heaped up with a believing heart.

What the chapter does not contain is a temple. There is no record in it of anything founded at the cave, in gratitude or otherwise. The Mahavamsa does record the building of a monastery of that name, but a long way further on and under a different king: in chapter XXXV, among the works of Amanda Gamani — Amandagamani Abhaya, son of Maha Dathika, who reigned nine years and eight months in the first century AD — comes the flat sentence 'and the ruler of men also built the Rajatalena-vihara', the monastery of the silver cave. The familiar account, in which Dutthagamani built this temple in gratitude for the silver, sent three hundred stone craftsmen and seven hundred other workers with his chief artisan, and brought a gold-plated image from India, is carried by later texts: chiefly the Ridi Vihara Asna, a Sinhala work, which also supplies the name Arahant Indragupta for the monk who showed the merchant the path and the episode in which that monk made the image fly through the air when the cart carrying it stuck between rocks. The Sri Lankan heritage literature records both attributions, notes that Amandagamani Abhaya is credited with construction, and says that Dutthagamani's founding is nonetheless widely accepted.

The site's own dated evidence begins with inscriptions and it does not begin with either king. Drip-ledged caves in the hill carry early Brahmi inscriptions in Old Sinhala of the second and first centuries BC, one of which reads as 'the cave of chief Tissa, son of the chief Punna, given to the Sangha'. A later Brahmi inscription of the first century AD, of the reign of Amanda Gamini Abhaya, records the donation of the villages Padagama and Kulagama, performed by pouring water from a golden vase. Another, of the second or third century AD, records a paddy field of nine karisa. A transitional Brahmi inscription of the fifth to seventh centuries records that Samanala of Patagala was freed from vaharala, with the merit conferred on all beings. So the earliest inscribed royal endowment at this site belongs to the same king the Mahavamsa credits with building the silver-cave monastery, and not to the king of the silver story.

The temple then disappears from the record for a long time, was in ruins, and was repaired in the eighteenth century under Kirti Sri Rajasinha, in whose reign the Uda Viharaya was added and almost everything now visible was painted or made. The monk that king appointed to continue the Culavamsa from its thirteenth-century state, Tibbatuwawe Buddharakkhita, was himself from this temple and described the restoration in it. The complex as it stands is small and various. A stone image house, the Waraka Welandu Viharaya — the shrine where the fruit was eaten — stands on the way in, with a mandapa of eight stone pillars carved with female dancers and a plan closer to a devala than to an image house, and Kandyan paintings inside. Past it an entrance hall holds a very large old alms bowl. The Maha Viharaya, also called the Pahala Viharaya, sits in the rock cave itself and holds a reclining figure about nine metres long, a gold-plated seated figure now kept under glass, figures of Ananda and of Maitreya, various devatas and one figure held by tradition to be Dutthagamani, and a row of five images reported once to have been gilded. The Uda Viharaya above it has three chambers and a corridor, with its best painting on the sides of the image's pedestal rather than on the walls: three lions sharing one head, a bull's and an elephant's head fused, armed figures read as a scene from the Rama and Ravana story, and, at the end of the cave, nine female figures arranged so that from a distance they make an elephant. There is an ivory-carved door frame with the Pancha Nari Ghataya, the pot of five women, and lion carvings beside it; a semicircular moonstone; two stupas, one behind the upper terrace and one on a separate rock called Serasumgala, believed to be where the earliest stupa stood; and two devalayas of the eighteenth-century revival.

And on the low altar at the foot of the reclining figure there are the tiles. About two hundred of them, blue on white, tin-glazed, eighteenth-century, Dutch, each one carrying an episode from the Hebrew and Christian scriptures. The scenes reported include the creation of man, the fall with the serpent in the garden, the expulsion from the garden, the flood and the dove with the olive branch, animals entering the ark two by two, Moses and the burning bush, prophets, the nativity, the transfiguration and the last supper. They are commonly called Delft tiles, and they are commonly said to have been given to Kirti Sri Rajasinha by a Dutch governor, who then offered them to the temple. No account found names the governor, gives a date, identifies an embassy or cites a document, Dutch or Sinhalese, and one Sri Lankan magazine account states plainly that the origin is undocumented and that the Dutch-governor attribution is a common belief. That reign also contained open war with the Dutch East India Company — Kandyan attacks on the Company's low-country forts from 1761, the Company's own campaign conventionally dated 1764 to 1766, its garrison withdrawing from the capital in 1765, and then the Treaty of 1766 negotiated by Governor Iman Willem Falck, under which the whole coastline was ceded to the Company. Nothing in the record consulted connects the tiles to any of it, in either direction. What is visible on the altar is agreed on by every account that describes it: the tiles are set in an order that follows nothing in the pictures, and a good many of them are sideways or upside down.

The temple is a protected monument, declared by government gazette notification of 11 August 1967. In 2008, during the pilgrimage season, a large section of the decorative plaster came off the cave roof, reportedly because of the heat of a crowd in a confined room.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concept in this group's second half is not about what anybody wanted. It is about the machinery of taking hold of something at all, and it names six factors that come and go and insists in its first sentence that none of them is good or bad in itself, each taking the colour of the mind it joins [C021-P:L25] [C021-M:L29]. This site exercises three of the six, and it exercises them as record rather than resemblance, which is the whole difference between this film and the one it replaced.

Start with the first factor. It is defined as what brings the mind and its co-arisen factors to the object and raises them onto it, and the Pradeepika's simile is exact and physical: another man helping you lift onto your shoulder a burden you could not have lifted by yourself [C021-P:L33]. The Margaya glosses the same factor as the effort that reaches where the mind has not reached and knows what was not known [C021-M:L7]. Now read the chronicle chapter. A huntsman went out with dogs after an iguana and found bricks. Fishermen found pearls on dry land. Villagers found gold in their own earth. And the merchant had loaded waggons for ginger, halted for whip-wood, cut one fruit, gave it away, and was then physically led to the silver by somebody else, along a path somebody else opened, with the chronicle stating the monk's purpose outright: 'in order to show him the silver'. Not one of the seven finders lifted his own object onto his own mind. That is the simile's content happening to seven different people on one day, in a text written down fifteen hundred years ago, and it is the reason this location was chosen over anything that merely looks like concentration.

The second factor the film uses is the deciding one, and the tiles are the only object on the slate that can stage it. The Pradeepika says it settles the object and helps the mind stand firmly on it without doubt, and then says something unusually blunt: without distinguishing true, false, good or bad, it takes hold of whatever the object may be and establishes it in the mind, and it very often does this wrongly, holding the untrue as true [C021-P:L45]. The Margaya adds that because of this factor the mind does not go two or three ways about a thing but takes it in some one way, rightly or wrongly, and that it is a hard-to-discern, unobvious factor [C021-M:L15]. Two hundred tiles were manufactured as decided objects — each one a picture with a chapter and verse behind it, made in quantity for the walls and fireplaces of houses on the other side of the world — and they arrived in a shrine where they were taken up as a surface for an altar, and laid down in whatever orientation a hand was holding them. The object did not change. What it is was settled somewhere else. And the film can say all of that without accusing anybody, because the source's wrongness clause is a clause about the factor: 'often wrong while being firm' is how minds work, not a finding about whoever laid this surface, and the digest's refusal of 'trust your gut, if you're sure it's right' is exactly that line. The inference that the tiler did not know what the pictures were is an inference in the modern literature and the film leaves it there.

The third factor is the one this group exists to separate from greed, and it is the ending. The Pradeepika is unambiguous: the wish to take the object up is one thing, and the power that makes one cling to the object is another, with its own names; by this factor only the taking of the object happens, without regard to good or bad [C021-P:L69]. The Margaya says it looks a little like greed but has none of greed's adhesion, and that in greed-accompanied minds it accords with greed while in minds set against greed it opposes it [C021-M:L27]; developed, it is said to subdue craving and to lead as far as a person can go [C021-P:L75]. A film in a group about the greed-rooted minds needs somewhere to say that a man who wanted ginger is not an exhibit, and this chapter is that place.

Then the feeling concept does two things the footage cannot. It puts a floor under a film whose middle is a dark surface: feeling is present in every mind because every mind arises taking an object [C032-P:L43], it is threefold by the way the object's flavour is experienced with no fourth way [C032-M:L5] [C032-P:L52], and fifty-five of the minds counted carry the neutral one [C032-M:L13] — which is not numbness, since the same neutral feeling runs through the most refined states in the scheme. And then it closes the film by limiting it. The Pradeepika divides suffering into the open and the concealed, and it gives the reason for the division rather than just the categories: the afflictions that arrive from outside, torment and violence and confinement, can be known without asking because the means of them is manifest [C032-P:L121], while pains of the head and the teeth and the limbs, and the burnings of a mind in desire or hatred, are concealed precisely because they have to be known by asking and their cause is not manifest [C032-P:L119]. This altar is faced with two hundred pictures of other people's extremity — an expulsion, a flood, a betrayal, a last meal — set where flowers are laid, in a room where people have knelt for centuries. Every one of those pictures is the open kind: a scene whose means is manifest, readable without asking. What any of it was to anybody who knelt there is the other kind, and the source says why it cannot be got at. It has to be asked for, and a camera does not ask. So the film's last move is off the surface and not into it, and the charge the sources make lands on the instrument rather than on anybody in the room.
what_is_certain: Mahavamsa chapter XXVIII, in Geiger's standard English translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, records seven appearances of material for the Great Thupa and states: 'In a southerly direction from the city, at a distance of eight yojanas, silver appeared in the Ambatthakola-cave.'

The same chapter gives the merchant's story in these terms: he had taken many waggons 'in order to bring ginger and so forth from Malaya'; he halted not far from the cave and 'since he had need of wood for whips he went up that mountain'; he found a branch of a bread-fruit tree 'bearing one single fruit as large as a waterpitcher'; he cut it and, 'thinking: I will give the first (produce as alms), with faith he announced the (meal) time'; four theras free from the asavas came and received bowls of the fruit's juice; four others came and received the kernels; three of those went their way and one did not, and 'in order to show him the silver he went further down and seating himself near the cave he ate the kernels'; the merchant followed his track, and 'the thera opened a path for him to the mouth of the cavern: Go thou now also on this path, lay brother!'; the merchant struck the silver with his axe, took a lump, left his waggons and went in haste to Anuradhapura and showed the king.

In the same chapter the other finds are also made by people about other business or none: the bricks, prepared by Vissakamma, are found by a huntsman who had gone into the forest with his dogs and pursued an iguana; gold nuggets on a sixteen-karisa plain near Acaravitthigama are noticed by the villagers; copper appears near Tambapittha; precious stones appear near the village of Sumanavapi; six waggonloads of pearls mingled with coral 'came forth to the dry land' at the landing-place Uruvela and are seen by fishermen; and four gems in a cave above the sand at the Pelivapikagama tank are seen by a hunter with his dogs. The king 'heard, on one and the same day, that the bricks and the other (treasures) had appeared for the Great Thupa'.

Mahavamsa chapter XXVIII contains no record of a temple, monastery or shrine being founded at the Ambatthakola cave, in gratitude or otherwise. Its closing verse is about merit heaped up with a believing heart.

Mahavamsa chapter XXXV, in the same translation, records among the works of Amanda Gamani — Amandagamani Abhaya, son of Maha Dathika, who reigned nine years and eight months — that 'the ruler of men also built the Rajatalena-vihara'.

The site's names are Rajata lena and Ridi Vihara, the silver cave and the silver temple; the Sri Lankan heritage literature gives its ancient name as Ambatthakola-lena and states that the chronicles refer to the temple as Rajata-lena.

The Sri Lankan heritage literature records four groups of inscriptions at the site: early Brahmi in Old Sinhala of the second to first centuries BC, one reading 'Parumaka-Puna-puta Parumaka tishaha lene shagasha', 'the cave of chief Tissa, son of the chief Punna, [is given] to Sangha'; later Brahmi of the first century AD, of the reign of Amanda Gamini Abhaya (22-31 AD), recording donations of the villages Padagama and Kulagama performed by pouring water from a golden vase; later Brahmi of the second to third centuries AD recording a paddy field of nine karisa at Vahamala Kariya; and transitional Brahmi of the fifth to seventh centuries AD recording that Samanala of Patagala was freed from vaharala with the merit conferred on all beings.

The temple was in ruins for a long period and was repaired and renovated under Kirti Sri Rajasinha, whose reign is given as 1747-1781 or 1747-1782. The Uda Viharaya was added in that reign, and most of the visible painting and sculpture is Kandyan.
Tibbatuwawe Buddharakkhita, the monk that king assigned to continue the Culavamsa from its thirteenth-century state, was from this temple and described the restoration in that continuation.

The complex includes: the Waraka Welandu Viharaya, a stone image house with a mandapa of eight stone pillars carved with female dancers, a plan and entrance hallway resembling a devala, and Kandyan wall paintings, whose name in Sinhala means the shrine in which the jackfruit was eaten; an entrance hall holding a very large old alms bowl; the Maha Viharaya or Pahala Viharaya in the rock cave, with a reclining Buddha image given as nine metres long, a gold-plated seated image now under a glass case, figures of Ananda Thera, Maitreya Bodhisattva and devatas, a figure held by tradition to be Dutthagamani, and a row of five images reported once gilded; the Uda Viharaya of three interconnected chambers and a linking corridor; an ivory-carved door frame bearing the Pancha Nari Ghataya, the pot of five women, with lion carvings; a semicircular sandakada pahana; two stupas, one beside a cave behind the upper terrace and one on a separate hill called Serasumgala, believed to be the site of the earliest stupa; and the Kumara Bandara and Paththini devalayas of the eighteenth-century revival.

The Uda Viharaya's distinctive painting is on the sides of the image's pedestal rather than on the walls: three lions sharing a single head (Tri Singha), a fused bull's and elephant's head (Vrushaba Kunjaraya), and armed figures read as a scene from the Rama and Ravana story. At the end of that cave is a painting of the Navanari Kunjaraya, nine female figures arranged so that from a distance they form an elephant.

The flower pedestal and altar at the foot of the reclining image is faced with Dutch tin-glazed tiles of the eighteenth century, blue on white, carrying scenes from the Bible, and known locally and in the heritage literature as 'Bible tiles'.
Every account that describes the tiles' arrangement reports that it follows nothing in the pictures and that a good many tiles are set sideways or upside down.

The site is an archaeological protected monument, declared by government gazette notification of 11 August 1967; the notification covers 'the rock with the inscription dating from B.C. to the early period of A.D. and the ancient cave temple belonging to the 1100-1800 A.D. period' at Rideegama village in the Ridigama Divisional Secretary's Division.
In 2008, during the pilgrimage season, a large section of the decorative plaster on the Maha Viharaya cave roof came off; the reason given is the heat of an overcrowded confined room.

Dutch tin-glazed tiles of this kind were made in several towns of the northern Netherlands rather than principally at Delft, from which the general reference literature says few tiles actually originated; biblical scenes were among the most popular motifs, often accompanied by a chapter and verse reference; and by the eighteenth century the tiles were made smaller and thinner so as to be cheaper to produce and to transport, with Dutch tile export continuing through that century.

Kirti Sri Rajasinha's reign included open war between the Kandyan kingdom and the Dutch East India Company: Kandyan attacks on Dutch low-country forts from 1761, a Company campaign conventionally dated 1764 to 1766, the Company's garrison abandoning the Kandyan capital in 1765, and the Treaty of 1766 negotiated by Governor Iman Willem Falck, by which the coastline was ceded to the Company.
what_is_disputed: The row's premise, and the commonest claim about this place, that the temple is recorded in the chronicles as built by Dutthagamani in gratitude for the silver. It is not in Mahavamsa XXVIII, which records the silver and no foundation; and Mahavamsa XXXV credits the building of the Rajatalena-vihara to Amandagamani Abhaya in the first century AD. The Dutthagamani account, with three hundred stone craftsmen and seven hundred other workers under the chief artisan, and the gold-plated image brought from India, comes from the Ridi Vihara Asna and from the Culavamsa as continued in the eighteenth century; secondary sources state that the Culavamsa carries it, but the passage was not located in this research and the claim rests on that assertion. The Sri Lankan heritage literature records both attributions and says Dutthagamani's founding is nonetheless widely accepted. The film treats the Dutthagamani foundation as tradition and states it as tradition.

The name of the monk. Mahavamsa XXVIII names none of the eight theras; the merchant meets two groups of four and one of the second group stays behind. The name Arahant Indragupta, the count of eight monks eating in sequence, and the episode in which that monk made a cart-bound image fly to the temple all come from the Ridi Vihara Asna and from later tradition, not from the chronicle passage.

The fruit. Geiger's translation reads bread-fruit throughout. The temple's own shrine name, Waraka Welandu Viharaya, and the whole Sinhala tradition say jackfruit, and one Sri Lankan heritage source states the discrepancy in as many words, calling the fruit jackfruit 'called breadfruit in the Mahavamsa translation'. Nothing here resolves which the Pali word means.

Whether the tiles were a gift from the Dutch, and from whom. 'A Dutch governor', 'a Dutch envoy' and 'a Dutch consul' are all in circulation. No account found names a governor, gives a date, identifies an embassy or cites any document, Dutch or Sinhalese, and one Sri Lankan magazine account says outright that the tiles' origin is undocumented and that the Dutch-governor attribution is a common belief. A search result also attached the gift to Governor Gustaaf Willem van Imhoff, whose governorship of 1736-1740 precedes Kirti Sri Rajasinha's accession in 1747, so that attribution is internally inconsistent and is not used. The film states that the tiles are Dutch and eighteenth-century and that how they arrived is not recorded, and goes no further.

How many tiles. About two hundred, in the Sri Lankan heritage literature and in the general reference literature; over a hundred, in a Sri Lankan magazine account describing the altar. No published count was found. The record uses 'about two hundred' and marks it approximate.

Where the tiles are. Reported variously as the flower pedestal supporting the reclining image; as the flower pedestal and the floor around it; as the platform beneath the reclining image; as the main flower altar; and, in one account, as the interior walls. The commonest and most specific description is the flower pedestal and altar at the foot of the reclining image, and the row's 'a floor of imported tiles' is one description among several rather than the established one. This needs checking on site before the film's central shot is planned.

Which scenes. Reported across the sources: the creation of man, the fall with the serpent in the garden, the expulsion from the garden, the flood and the dove with the olive branch, animals entering the ark two by two, Moses and the burning bush, prophets, the nativity, the transfiguration, the last supper, and in one account the crucifixion. The lists differ and no catalogue of the set was found. The film names only scenes reported by more than one source.

The inference that whoever laid the tiles did not know what the pictures were. Two accounts draw it from the haphazard arrangement. It is an inference in those accounts and not a record, and the film does not state or imply it.

'Delft'. The tiles are commonly called Delft tiles and one account ascribes them to 'the 18th century Delft factory in Holland'. Dutch tin-glazed tiles of the period were made in several northern towns, and the general reference literature says few tiles came from Delft itself. No maker, town or year has been established for this set.

The coordinates. OpenStreetMap gives 7.5367 N, 80.4914 E for the temple on Ridee Vihara Road at Rideegama; the general reference literature gives 7 degrees 33 minutes north, 80 degrees 29 minutes east, that is 7.55 and 80.4833, rounded to the arc-minute and about 1.7 km away. The mapped point is used here and neither has been verified on the ground.

The distance from the district town. Eighteen, nineteen, twenty and twenty-one kilometres are all in print, the last of them explicitly as a road distance by way of Mallawapitiya; the straight-line distance from the town centre to the mapped point is about fifteen kilometres. The figures measure different things and are not reconciled. The row's '18 km north-east' is in the right region; the bearing from the town is closer to east-north-east.
The reclining image. Nine metres is given by two sources and is used. One visitor account calls the reclining image 'from Burma', which nothing else found supports and which is not used.

The gold-plated image. That it is about 2,200 years old, that it was brought from India, and that it was installed as an offering of gratitude, are traditional claims; the episode of its flying to the temple is in the Ridi Vihara Asna. None is treated as established.

The number of caves. About twenty-five caves said to have been occupied by arahants since the third century BC is a traditional figure from the general reference literature; the Sri Lankan heritage literature speaks of drip-ledged caves without giving a total.

Bees. One caving source records colonies of Apis dorsata nesting beneath the boulder overhang, together with a local belief that those who enter with impure hearts are stung. No other source found mentions it. It is recorded because it bears on access and on a crew standing still under an overhang, not because it is established.

Conservation. Beyond the 2008 plaster loss, the encasing of the gold-plated image in glass and reported past vandalism of the ivory carving and other pieces, no conservation report, condition survey or restoration programme for the tiles, the paintings or the cave roof was found, and the tiles' present condition is known here only from visitor photographs and descriptions.

what_to_film: The approach in flat early light, from the ground and without a drone: a low grey rock hill with nothing monumental in it, held long, so that the film's scale is established as small before anything is found.
The stone image house on the way in: the eight carved pillars in raking light, the carved figures at eye level, the low ceiling, and the empty hall beyond it with the old alms bowl standing in it.
The mouth of the rock cave and the fall-off of light behind it, exposed on available light so the darkness is the real darkness.
The whole length of the reclining figure in one static frame from floor level, on doorway light alone, with the far end of it going.

The single shot the film exists for: one slow lateral pass along the tiled face of the altar in the first raking light, close enough to read tile after tile, in one unbroken move, at whatever the morning actually gives. It needs minutes and it has no substitute.
Macro on single tiles, available light: the glaze, the crazing, the pooled blue at the end of a brushstroke, a corner chipped away. Nothing touched, nothing cleaned, nothing wetted.
The tiles that are set sideways or inverted, filmed exactly as they lie, with no marking, arrow, overlay or rotation of the frame to point them out.
The altar in full as the light leaves it, until the blue goes dark and the pictures stop being legible. This is the film's long middle and it is not cut short.
The lift: the camera rising a metre off the surface in one move so the two hundred pictures become a field of blue and white. The payoff, and it is a move rather than a shot.
The ivory-carved door frame and the semicircular moonstone, small and flat on, in the same available light.
The stupa on its separate rock from below, in flat light, one static frame, as the way out.
Sound recorded on its own: the room's own quiet, and what comes in through the opening from outside.
suggested_location.access: By road from the district town, out past Mallawapitiya and along the Keppitigala road, then about 1.5 km on a signposted side road; reported at 18 to 21 km from the town depending on the source and the route. This is a living temple under the Malwatte chapter, not a monument with an entrance regime, so access to the shrines is a matter of the resident community's agreement and, separately, the heritage authority's, and neither has been sought. Shoes are removed and shoulders and knees covered. The shrine interiors are entered off a terrace reached by steps, and the Uda Viharaya by further steps behind the lower shrine; the stupa on Serasumgala has its own granite flight. The interiors are dim and the only honest light is what comes through the openings: the cave roof carries painted plaster that has already come down once in a crowded season and the tiles are a two-hundred-year-old glaze, so flash and every substitute for it are treated here as prohibited, and nothing is touched. Drone is treated as prohibited outright and the film is built so that it never needs one. Pilgrimage-season crowding is heavy enough to have damaged the roof, so the film cannot be attempted then. One caving source reports colonies of Apis dorsata nesting beneath the boulder overhang, which matters for a crew standing still under it. Filming inside may simply be refused, and in that case this record does not have a smaller version: the altar is the film.
suggested_location.best_time: First light on an ordinary weekday, out of the pilgrimage season and never on a full-moon observance day. The one shot the film is built on needs low sun raking along the tiled face of the altar through the shrine's opening, so the window is short, it is at one end of the day, and it needs a clear morning; in flat light the pass does not exist. Nothing else here depends on season, weather or month. The orientation of the shrine's opening has not been confirmed against a plan, so whether the raking light arrives in the morning or the evening is an assumption that has to be checked on site before anything is scheduled.
