suggested_location.research_note: Desk research by web search only, on 26 September 2026; nothing checked on the ground, in an archive or against a printed edition. The chronicle passages are the strongest thing in this record and they are first-hand: the full text of Mahavamsa chapters XXVIII and XXXV was read in Geiger's standard English translation as published at lakdiva.org.lk, and every quotation here is taken from that text rather than from a secondary paraphrase. That reading is also what produced the corrections. Chapter XXVIII records the silver in the Ambatthakola cave and contains no foundation of any temple; the merchant is travelling for ginger and stops for whip-wood; the fruit is a bread-fruit in that translation; the theras are two groups of four and are unnamed; and the chapter's other six finds are all made by people about other business. Chapter XXXV attributes the building of the Rajatalena-vihara to Amandagamani Abhaya in the first century AD. The Dutthagamani-in-gratitude account, the craftsmen, the imported image, the name Arahant Indragupta and the flying-statue episode are traced in the secondary sources to the Ridi Vihara Asna and to the Culavamsa as continued; the Culavamsa passage itself could not be located, since the online text used carries only the Mahavamsa proper, so the assertion that the Culavamsa carries the foundation rests on secondary statement and is recorded as such. The most careful source used for the site itself is the Sri Lankan heritage literature at lankapradeepa.com, which is the basis for the four inscription groups and their readings and datings, the structures, the ancient name Ambatthakola-lena, the double attribution of the foundation, the Culavamsa continuation by a monk of this temple, and the gazette notification of 11 August 1967; the gazette number 14761 appears in that source's own wording and was not checked against the gazette. The tiles are where the research is thinnest and the record says so. Every figure and every attribution differs between accounts: about two hundred tiles in two sources and over a hundred in a third; the flower pedestal, the pedestal and floor, the platform, the main altar and even the interior walls as their location; a Dutch governor, a Dutch envoy and a Dutch consul as the donor, with no name, no date, no embassy and no document in any of them; and one Sri Lankan magazine account stating outright that the origin is undocumented and the Dutch-governor attribution a common belief. One search result attached the gift to Governor van Imhoff, whose governorship ended seven years before Kirti Sri Rajasinha's accession, which is self-contradictory and is not used. 'Delft' is treated as a loose trade name on the strength of the general reference literature, which states that few tiles were actually made at Delft and that Dutch tile production of the period was spread across several northern towns; no maker, town or year for this set was found anywhere. The scenes listed are only those reported by more than one source. That many tiles are sideways or inverted is reported by more than one visitor account and is the film's central observation, so it needs confirming in person before anything is committed; the further inference that the tiler did not know what the pictures were is an inference in those accounts and is held in what_is_disputed. The coordinates used, 7.5367 north and 80.4914 east, are an OpenStreetMap point for the temple on Ridee Vihara Road at Rideegama; the general reference literature's 7 degrees 33 minutes by 80 degrees 29 minutes is rounded to the arc-minute and sits about 1.7 km away, and neither has been verified on the ground. No elevation is recorded because no figure for the shrine terrace was found and the hill's height above the surrounding country is nowhere given. The 2008 plaster loss and the bee colonies under the overhang each come from a single source and are recorded as such because they bear on access and on standing still in that room. Six Commons files were confirmed through action=query&titles= before their URLs were written, and about sixty were reviewed across four searches and the site category; no file on Commons was found whose description says it shows the tiles, so the five site images written in show the cave, the interior, the stone image house, the ivory carving and the moonstone, and the sixth is explicitly captioned as an object-type reference from a museum and not as this temple. The Lonely Planet page returned only navigation to fetching and contributed nothing beyond its presence in the source list. Access, community and heritage permission, whether a camera is allowed in the shrine at all, tripod rules, the orientation of the shrine's opening and therefore the time of day the raking light arrives, and the months of the pilgrimage season, are all unverified.

unknowns: No permission of any kind has been sought or found. This is a living temple and a protected monument, and filming inside the shrine needs the resident community's agreement and the heritage authority's; either may be refused outright, and everything here is a research direction.

Whether the tiles are on the flower pedestal, on the altar, on the floor around the reclining image, or on some combination of those, is reported inconsistently, and the film's central shot depends on knowing which. It has not been checked.

Whether low raking light reaches the tiled face at all, and at which end of the day, is an inference from the site's general description and has not been checked against a plan or on site. The one shot the film exists for depends on it.
Whether the interiors can be exposed at all on available light with the equipment this series uses is untested, and nothing in this film may be lit.

The number of tiles, the scenes on them, their present condition and whether any published catalogue or survey of them exists are all unknown; no conservation report for the tiles, the roof plaster or the paintings was found.
How the tiles arrived is not recorded in anything found. No archival search, Dutch or Sinhalese, has been attempted, and a real archive search might settle it either way.
The months of the pilgrimage season, and therefore which parts of the year the room is too crowded to film in, were not established.
Whether a tripod, or a stationary operator, is permissible beside an altar on which flowers are being set is unknown, and the film's slow lateral pass assumes it.
This record puts a sixth film in one district. The six are separated by period, kind of place and treatment, but the concentration is a slate-level judgement and is flagged rather than resolved.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location is Claude's suggestion and awaits Chathura's verdict; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
